summary: Documents experiences with the RFC 1797 experiment in subnetting a class A network, run by the Net39 Test Group, and gives recommendations to the Internet registries and the operations community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Large blocks of IP addresses used to be given out whole. This memo reports a test in which part of one such block was split into smaller pieces and shared, and it lists the problems that turned up for the people running the network. It concludes that the split worked, as long as the pieces are handed out under the usual rules.

subtitle: What happened when a slice of a Class A network was handed out as subnets, and what routers needed.

tldr.problem: Class A address space had not been split into smaller subnets across providers, and it was not known whether routers and operations would cope.
tldr.mechanism: The Net39 Test Group delegated subnets under the RFC 1797 experiment, ran common services over them, and recorded the routing, registry and operational problems that appeared.
tldr.outcome: The memo calls the experiment a success and says it is safe to start carving up Class A space if the pieces are handed out under normal Internet Registry conventions, and asks IANA to consider this for future delegations.

facts.label: Aggregate sent instead of the subnet

today: RFC 1879 is an Informational memo from January 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It reports on the experiment defined in RFC 1797, and its recommendations are aimed at the Internet registries and the network operations community of that time.

sections.title: The Experiment and What It Ran
sections.content:
This memo documents experiences with the RFC 1797 subnet A experiment, performed by the Net39 Test Group, and gives recommendations for the Internet Registries and the operations community. Not all of the experiments proposed in RFC 1797 were carried out: only the "case one" type delegations were made. Additional work was done inside the DNS service, by supporting a root name server and the primary server for the domain from within the subnetted address space, and testing was done on classless delegation.

The Internet services offered over the experiment were Finger, HTTP, Telnet, an FTP server and client, Gopher, kerberos, lpr and its relatives, X, and DNS. A root name server, F.Root-Servers.Net, had an interface defined as part of the experiment, and its operator reported its performance: 400,000,000 queries processed in 38 days, with well over half of them going to the temporary 39.13.229.241 address. He kept the old 192.5.5.241 address as well, because he knew a lot of people would not update their root.cache files and he did not want to create a black hole.
sections.plainLanguage: A test group took part of a very large block of addresses, split it into smaller pieces, and handed the pieces out. Real services ran on it, including a root name server that answered a very large number of queries.

sections.title: Operational Problems
sections.content:
Early predictions seemed to indicate that the safest path for a provider taking part in such a routing system is to have all of its clients either singly connected to one upstream provider, or running a classless interior routing protocol. The memo also notes that a network with a default route may not notice it has potential routing problems until it starts using subnets of traditional Class A networks internally.

There were initial problems in at least one RIPE181 implementation. It is clear that operators need to register in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR) all active aggregates and delegations for any given prefix, and that there need to be methods for determining who is authoritative for announcing any given prefix. The memo expects the problems found inside this experiment to apply to some RFC 1597 prefixes or to any "natural" Class A space.

Use of traceroute with loose source routing was critical for troubleshooting during the experiment. In current cisco IOS, the statement no ip source-route disables loose source routing and so hinders cross-provider troubleshooting, so the memo recommends that this statement not be placed in active ISP cisco configurations. It also notes, without resolving them, serious weaknesses in the inter-provider cooperation model, and suggests that the IEPG or the national and continental operations bodies might take this on as an action item.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbouring network operators have to record who owns which slice of addresses, and they have to keep their debugging tools switched on so that they can help each other find faults.

sections.title: Routing Problems and the Fixes
sections.content:
A classic cisco configuration that contains ip route 39.1.28.0 255.255.255.0, router bgp 64000 and redistribute static will, by default, promote any classful subnet route to a full classful route. Supernet routes are left alone. The behaviour can be changed in at least two ways, by adding no auto-summary or by using a network statement with a mask together with a route map and an access list.

Users of cisco gear currently need to code two more statements: ip classless and ip subnet-zero. The first directive removes the idea that if you know how to talk to a subnet of a network you know how to talk to all of the network. The second is needed because it is no longer clear where the all-ones or all-zeros networks are.

Other infrastructure gear behaved similarly or worse. Equipment that depends on a classful routing protocol, such as RIPv1, is prone to misconfiguration. The tested examples are current Ascend and Livingston gear, which continue to use RIPv1 as the default or only routing protocol, and RIPv1 use creates an aggregate announcement. The problem showed up when an Ascend and a cisco were asked to talk to each other: the Ascend was told to announce 39.1.28/24, but since RIPv1 cannot do this, the Ascend sent 39/8 instead. The memo notes that RIPv1, as with all classful interior gateway protocols, should be considered historic, and that this confirms the earlier predictions.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older routers only understood whole big blocks, so when asked to announce one small slice, they announced the entire block. Newer settings teach routers to handle small slices correctly.

sections.title: Three Ways to Fix the Aggregation Problem
sections.content:
There are three ways to solve the unintended aggregation problem with current cisco IOS, and which one applies depends on the software version in the router. Workarounds exist even for ancient software such as version 8.X.

The preferred solution is to turn on ip classless in the routers and use a default route inside the autonomous system. The ip classless command prevents the existence of a single subnet route from blocking access via the default route to other subnets of the same old-style network. This default route only works with single-homed ISPs.

The workaround for version 9.1 or later software, where ip classless is not available, is to install a default network route such as ip route 39.0.0.0 255.0.0.0 <next-hop> along the axis the default route would normally take. It appears an ISP can use recursive route lookups, so the next hop need not be a directly connected neighbour, and the internal router can point to a loopback interface on the border router. The memo warns that this can become "really uncomfortably messy" and that a distribute-list may be needed to prevent the announcement of the shorter mask. For version 9.0 or older software, create a default subnet route, ip route 39.x.y.0 <next-hop>, combined with ip default-network 39.x.y.0, otherwise as in the 9.1 fix.

Both of the latter solutions rely on manual configuration, and in the long run they will be impossible to maintain. In some topologies the use of manual configuration can be a problem, for example where there is more than one possible exit point from the autonomous system to choose from.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a preferred setting, and two older ones for machines that do not support it. The two older ones need a human to keep them up to date, which the memo says will not work in the long run.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The memo's conclusion is that the RFC 1797 experiment appears to have been a success. It believes it safe to start carving up Class A space, if the spaces are delegated according to normal Internet Registry conventions, and it recommends that IANA consider this for future address delegations.

The Security Considerations section says security issues were not considered in this experiment. The memo closes with credits to the RFC 1797 participants and to the organizations that took part, and with a list of the references the experiment relied on.
sections.plainLanguage: The report's answer is yes, you can split up the big blocks, as long as the pieces are handed out under the usual rules for handing out addresses.

viz.caption: THE CONFIGURATION THAT PROMOTES A SUBNET ROUTE TO A FULL CLASSFUL ROUTE

data.title: cisco configuration
data.code:
ip route 39.1.28.0 255.255.255.0
router bgp 64000
redistribute static

viz.caption: THE SETTINGS AND CHOICES THE MEMO TALKS ABOUT

items.title: ip classless
items.text: Removes the idea that knowing one subnet means knowing the whole network.

items.title: ip subnet-zero
items.text: Needed because it is no longer clear where the all-ones and all-zeros networks are.

items.title: no auto-summary
items.text: Stops the router from promoting a subnet route into a full classful route.

items.title: no ip source-route
items.text: Disables loose source routing, so do not put it in an active ISP configuration.

items.title: RIPv1
items.text: A classful protocol that cannot carry a longer prefix; the memo calls it historic.

items.title: IRR registration
items.text: Register every active aggregate and delegation for a prefix, and know who may announce it.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO STOP THE UNINTENDED AGGREGATION

cells: ip classless with a default route
The default route works only with single-homed ISPs
May need a distribute-list to stop the shorter mask
ip route 39.x.y.0 next-hop with ip default-network
